XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Gwasanaethau Cyhoeddus yng Nghefn Gwlad Cymru
1. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o ddarpariaeth gwasanaethau cyhoeddus yng nghefn gwlad Cymru? OQ64619
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 1. What assessment has the First Minister made of the provision of public services in rural Wales? OQ64619

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Prynhawn da i chi i gyd.

We are focused on making services better in every part of Wales. We recognise that delivering effective public services in rural Wales requires responding to the particular challenges that rural communities face. Our proposal for a statutory rural-proofing duty will improve how the needs of rural communities are accounted for in how services are designed and in how they're delivered.

Thank you, First Minister. During the election campaign, I heard the same concern right across the Gwynedd Maldwyn constituency that rural mid Wales is too often overlooked. We're seeing schools close, continuing problems on the Cambrian line, in-patient beds closed at Tywyn, and potentially fewer community hospital beds provided in Powys. This winter we are also facing reductions in routine gritting. Now, I know the response: 'Schools and roads are matters for councils, health services for health boards'. But the Welsh Government sets policy, provides much of the funding and can intervene. Indeed, you've just provided Powys Teaching Health Board with an additional £3.5 million to tackle waiting lists. So, who in your Government is responsible for looking at the cumulative effect of all these decisions on rural communities, and what are you going to do about it?

As I said, this is something that this Government has proposed specific action to address. We want to be a Government for all of Wales. I agree that there are times where it has felt as if the specific needs of rural areas, rurality itself, hasn't been taken into account when decisions are being made. That is precisely what the rural-proofing mechanism is about. We are proposing to legislate on rural-proofing to make sure that it is not up to the Government of the day whether or not they take into account the impact of decisions on rural areas, but that that is put on a statutory basis. I think that is something that will be welcomed in rural parts of Wales.

Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Access to essential services is a major concern for many of my constituents in Monmouthshire, and the statistics back that up. Some of the most pressing issues found in the Welsh index of multiple deprivation statistics include access to pharmacies, GPs, local shops and childcare. These services are often twice as hard to reach in rural areas as the national average. The challenges are hard to tackle, but there are communities working to do this. What is the Welsh Government doing to address these wide-ranging problems in rural areas like Monmouthshire?

What the Member does, again, is emphasise a number of those issues on which there are particular questions that relate more to rural areas than to urban areas. We could point to the price of fuel now, which is problematic for everybody in Wales. The UK Government has taken the decision to have a rural relief system in place for some parts of the UK, but not for Wales. That's something that I would like to see the UK Government address. What our proposal, through the rural-proofing legislation route, will do for Wales is make sure that all those questions of rurality, as I say, are considered when it comes to decisions that the Welsh Government makes, because, whoever they are in whatever part of Wales, the electors who sent all of us here should feel that we are there for them.

You touched on the price of fuel, First Minister, and your desire to see the rural-proofing relief scheme activated again. Has your Government put any pressure on the UK Government to bring this forward in the budget that is going to come at the end of October? If you have, can you release that letter or whatever correspondence you've put in to support that? The Treasury model shows that anything between 20 per cent and 60 per cent is the sparsity premium that is put on the delivery of rural services, and help with the price of fuel will go a long way to relieving that pressure.

The Member will know that it has been a long-standing policy of the party that I lead to pursue that kind of rural relief. Our pressure on the UK Government has tended to, for obvious reasons, target energy prices and household fuel in particular, and calling for measures around off-grid as one of those elements that affect those living in more rural areas most. But there's no question now, as the intensity of the pressures of fuel for road users becomes more serious, that we will pursue that indeed with the UK Government.

Prynhawn da, Brif Weinidog. Just to come back to Powys, and to health services, you'll know that the Powys teaching health board has launched a proposal and a consultation on the future of health services across Powys. These proposals include cuts to hospital beds, which would leave communities like Ystradgynlais with a 23-mile journey to receive in-patient care. In a large rural county with poor public transport, as you will know, that matters enormously to patients, families and carers.

Nine thousand, seven hundred people have signed our petition opposing these plans, yet their voices are being brushed aside, and they are repeatedly told by your Government, and the health board, to simply wait for the consultation to finish. But the options on the table mean that significant reductions in in-patient care are already baked in, and that that consultation only presents one option.

We've been told that your Government can't do anything, but we know that the Welsh Government has mechanisms to intervene when it needs to, for example, with the fire and rescue services.
A question, please, Jane.
So, what will your Government do in order to listen to the voices of people in a rural area like Powys and make sure that these proposals are stopped? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

I'm certainly hearing the concerns, and the argument that has been put forward by the Member today amplifies concerns that have been raised elsewhere. This is a decision for the health board, of course, and consultation has begun on proposed options for its clinical services plan. Evidence can be seen. Views can be shared, experiences and concerns shared, alternative ideas put forward too. 

The health board has made no decisions on those clinical plans, but the Welsh Government—let me put it as clearly as I can—expects the health board to make evidence-based decisions, underpin those decisions on robust options appraisals and impact assessments, to ensure that the future of services are sustainable, fit for purpose and safe for the local population.

But, other than that, given that this is an ongoing process led by the health board, it would be inappropriate for me to comment more than that.
Swyddfeydd Rhyngwladol
2. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog amlinellu sut mae swyddfeydd rhyngwladol Llywodraeth Cymru yn darparu gwerth am arian i drethdalwyr Cymru? OQ64621
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 2. Will the First Minister outline how the Welsh Government’s international offices deliver value for money for Welsh taxpayers? OQ64621

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I have always vowed, as an internationalist, that my Government will be internationalist in its outlook and always seek opportunities to sell Wales to the world. Through our overseas network, we have opportunities to support exports, to attract inward investment, but also to strengthen international partnerships and to promote Wales. And like all aspects of Government, we will want, as a new Government, to make sure that our operations in this area are effective and efficient.

International relations are not the remit of the Welsh Government. Coming from the world of farming and business before entering the Senedd, when I came here I was shocked at the waste—it really shocked me. And nothing symbolises that waste more than the 20 mini embassies that we've got. These are on four continents, costing £5 million a year to run, and they're part of a larger package of £58 million, which is spent on all sorts of things. Is this indulgence worth it when public finances are so tight? 

So, does the First Minister genuinely believe that every one of those overseas offices is delivering value for money? And would he not agree with me that the money would be better spent on the NHS, schools and other failing vital public services that are actually within the Senedd's devolved responsibilities?

Spending money on all sorts of things is quite an argument to put forward. 

I'll tell you what the Welsh Government is absolutely meant to do by law. It is to seek the best for Wales. Our international operations are about seeking trade deals for Wales, attracting inward investment to Wales, selling agriculture produce to the world, building the kind of soft diplomacy that can bring results to Wales. 

Now, I know that the Members is isolationist in the way that he sees the world.

Now, I know that the Member is isolationist in the way that he sees the world. I am not; I am somebody who will always seek to promote Wales's place in the world for the benefit of all the people who live in Wales.

Prif Weinidog, as you've outlined, discussions about our international offices too often reduce them to a line in a budget, as if a desk abroad is simply a cost to be defended. But as you said, an office is not just a desk, it's a doorway. The relationships we build with Governments and organisations overseas translate into direct benefits for the Welsh economy: trade routes opened, investment attracted, markets found for Welsh businesses, which no amount of domestic marketing can replicate. I don't know if that was an experience of the business owner, of the Member over there.

So, in an increasingly interconnected world, I believe that we must think global and act local, learning not only from our neighbours in Scotland and Ireland, but from all across the world. That's why programs such as Taith's international learning exchanges are so important in forging those connections. So, may I ask if you agree with me, First Minister, that Welsh Government international offices should be measured not only in monetary value, but in the relationships they build—relationships that deliver real economic benefits for the people of Wales?

Thank you for the question. The groans from the Reform benches when the Member mentioned Wales having a doorway to the world I think speaks volumes about a party that wants to close all opportunities for Wales. This Government, as I say, will be international in its outlook, international in the kind of ambition that we have in our goals. Wales can't just be promoted from behind a desk in Cardiff, or by looking inwards. Our international offices shouldn't be judged either solely by trade and investment figures, though they are important. They also build trust, they deepen relationships, and they deliver results in soft power and in cultural diplomacy. Through our engagement across Europe and beyond—again, something that the Reform benches want to close down—Wales is sharing expertise on language, where we are global leaders in many ways, on sustainability, on future generations, while learning from others and delivering benefits for the people of Wales in doing so.

First Minister, shouldn't value for money, as you say, be not just measured by—and the cost; all of that has been discussed—investment, jobs, opportunities, but also what communities then locally get back as well? You've mentioned a range of different things, but how do we then ensure that those economic benefits are genuinely felt across all of our communities in Wales?

I agree with that outlook—that our international links can and must bring real benefits to the people of Wales. I enjoyed my participation with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association over 10 years as Chair. I assume that Reform want us to pull out of the work of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, as that's a waste of time looking out to the world. But what we were doing always was trying to find that common ground with others that can give us tools to do the job to improve the lot of people in Wales. That's what we're all about: it all has to come back to improving outcomes. Whilst I have a great belief in what we can do well here in Wales, I absolutely believe that, out there in the world, there are a host of lessons, a host of experiences that can come to us from different cultures that we can benefit from. That's something that I will always strive to work across party boundaries here in the Senedd on.

First Minister, the irony of you calling a Member of the Senedd an isolationist when you are desperate to break up the United Kingdom and isolate Wales from this United Kingdom, when you've signed a pact with the SNP and Sinn Féin to isolate Wales from the rest of the United Kingdom; the irony of that, First Minister.

The reality on the ground, First Minister, is that there are people being treated in corridors in our hospitals, our roads are creaking, our businesses are being taxed to the hilt. These aren't just slogans, First Minister. I met with my residents in Bretton and Broughton last week, who were flooded in 2021, they were flooded in 2023, they were flooded in 2025. How can you look them in the eye, First Minister, and tell them money's being better spent in international offices in places like China rather than on flood defences in places like Bretton and Broughton?

I think your leader had his head in his hands, trying to put distance between himself and Reform, and there we are—banging the tables on the Reform benches at your isolationist arguments for Wales. The Member knows full well that Government, to use the kind of detail that we heard earlier, does many, many things. In reaching out to the world

In reaching out to the world for trade deals, for lessons, for the sharing of experiences, we are adding to that depth of knowledge that we have and the income that we have in order to improve the lives of the people of Wales. We do that alongside improving the health service, improving education standards, improving job prospects in all parts of Wales, rolling out the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the UK and also dealing with those challenges of climate change, which my party is making a clear priority.
Galwaf yn awr ar arweinwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Prif Weinidog. Yn gyntaf, arweinydd Reform UK, Helen Jenner.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: I now call on the party leaders to question the First Minister. First, the leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. Before I begin, may I congratulate Welshman Elfyn Evans on becoming world rally champion after a nail-biting finale in Sardinia on Sunday? What a proud moment for Wales and what a wonderful sight to see y ddraig goch flying on the world stage.

First Minister, I want to pay tribute to our Jewish community in Wales and across the United Kingdom, particularly in light of the 7 October anniversary tomorrow. Jewish people do not feel safe in this country and for that, the establishment should feel deeply ashamed. There is a sickening antisemitism problem among left-wing parties. We've seen it in Labour, we've seen it in Plaid, and just last weekend, the Green Party of England and Wales formally adopted a policy saying Zionism is racism. The Greens officially do not want the State of Israel to exist, and Plaid Cymru has shamefully stood shoulder to shoulder with the Greens and their anti-Israel rhetoric. First Minister, during the election campaign, you claimed you had the most in common with the Greens, but in light of them formally adopting this divisive direction, I would ask: do you believe that supporting the existence of a Jewish state is in itself racist—'yes' or 'no'?

I have always advocated the two-state solution, and I think the decision taken at the Greens conference was ill judged. I do not agree with that motion.

I have to, though, refer to the initial comments that the Member made about Elfyn Evans. I spoke with Elfyn yesterday and congratulated him on his remarkable win and becoming the first Welsh world rally champion after coming so close on five previous occasions. And I'm sure the Member doesn't miss the irony in the way that she put the question in congratulating him for flying the Welsh flag on a world stage, when previously this afternoon, we had been asked to take down that Welsh flag and just look inwards. That is Reform's view of Wales.
So, that was what you chose to focus on in your response—
No. I answered your question.
—rather than condemning—. That was what you went for.
I answered your question. Llywydd, I answered the question.

The prelude, not the actual question. First Minister, it's quite clear that once again, your party is on the wrong side of history in failing to stand up for our vulnerable Jewish community.

Another example of Plaid being on the wrong side of history is Brexit. Wales voted decisively to leave the European Union, with almost twice as many people in Wales voting for Brexit than for Plaid Cymru in May. First Minister, at your conference last weekend, your party was making the case for rejoining the EU. Not only do you want to divide families by banging on about independence, you're now trying to reopen the Brexit debate. The so-called Party of Wales is clearly more keen on giving up Welsh sovereignty to Brussels than respecting the will of the people of Wales, who voted to leave the European Union.

Take farming. Brexit gave the Senedd the power to design and implement farming policy in Wales for Wales. First Minister, if you don't trust yourself with the powers you have, rather than seek to hand them over to Brussels, why don't you hand them over to us? Because we're ready to take the reins.

I think it's important to put it on the record so that the leader of Reform can read it afterwards, as she wasn't listening to me previously, that I directly addressed her question on the vote in the Green Party conference, and I said that I had a very, very different view, and that I believe in a two-state solution and I stand shoulder to shoulder with the Jewish communities in Wales and make a stand against antisemitism as I do Islamophobia.

She's on a roll. A second ago, she was saying that it was okay for a sportsman to wave the Welsh flag, but not for the rest of us to—or for Welsh Government to do so. And now she has the boldness—

And now she has the boldness—and I've suggested she's bold before—to suggest that, 10 years on from Brexit, the evidence shows that it was the right thing to do. Now, I'm not one to question the decision made by people in that specific referendum 10 years ago, but I am very, very clear in my mind that the damage that has been caused is very, very clear to see. She told me, 'Take farming'. Well, Brexit took too much out of farming. It took too much out of business. It is because of the losses that businesses face, the billions of pounds that have been lost to the Welsh economy, that I say that Wales's place is at the heart of Europe. As an absolute minimum, we should be members of the common market; we should be members of the customs union. That is in the interest of the people of Wales. The Reform leader, we know, takes a different viewpoint: she is isolationist in many, many ways. I will stand up for the people of Wales, as I pledged I would in the recent election.

First Minister, it's clear to anybody with an ounce of common sense that the reason anybody can say anything negative about the post-Brexit era is because the people who were in charge of seeing it through didn't make the most of the opportunities they were given. And I would like to quote. [Interruption.] I would like to quote. He talks about our relationship with Europe, the greatest Briton that ever lived, Winston Churchill, once said:

'We are with Europe but not of it. We are linked, not combined. We are interested and associated, not absorbed.'

First Minister, at your conference you spoke about a new deal for Wales. Well, the public aren't daft. What we're actually getting is a raw deal. You're giving Wales a raw deal by failing to grow our economy. Unemployment is up, and not a week goes by without a negative story of businesses in Wales shutting up shop and cutting jobs. And the education sector is in such a dire state that teaching unions are threatening industrial action against this Government. What have you done to turn the dire situation around? Nothing. Instead of making substantive cuts to business taxes and energy costs by scrapping net stupid zero, you're marching for separatism in Aberystwyth. Your programme for government was thin and without measurable targets. When are you going to ditch the dodgy ideology and start putting people first? Because so far, all you've done is make things worse.

I'm sure I just heard the leader of Reform accusing me of having dodgy ideology when she literally used the words 'net stupid zero'. Now, that is climate change ideological madness wrapped up in the words of the leader of Reform here in the Senedd. There's too much to unpack in that question for me to address all issues, but I will say this: she says that Brexit hasn't worked because the leaders, on a UK level, didn't get it right. At least I'm glad that she accepts that Brexit hasn't worked. That is why we need to look again at our relationship with Europe and tightening up that relationship for the interests of businesses in Wales and all our citizens.
Arweinydd Llafur Cymru, Ken Skates.

Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, Robin Hood took from the rich and gave to the poor, but I fear your Government is about to do the opposite. I'm afraid that cuts are being promised, Flying Start has been put on notice, and £10 weekly payments for the poorest haven't happened yet. You're pressing ahead with free childcare for millionaires, just like the Tories wish to do. Can you tell us how much people earning more than £100,000 a year will benefit from, through your childcare policy?

So, there are no cuts to Flying Start. We are building greatly on Flying Start in rolling out the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the UK, and we believe in the principle of universalism. I'm surprised that this is the second bite of the cherry from the Labour leader in Wales in undermining those principles of universalism that have given us the NHS, those principles of universalism that previous Labour Governments have celebrated, through free bus passes, through prescriptions. Is the Labour leader in Wales now suggesting that he, if he were in Government, would take away those elements of universalism that have been so well embraced by the people of Wales in recent years?

Well, the First Minister knows full well that we would never ever do that, and it's simply a deflection from the truth. Because I can reveal what the cost to the taxpayer would be in giving millionaires and the highest earners free childcare: it would amount to about £15 million per year. For every person earning over £100,000 a year, they would benefit from Plaid Cymru's Government to the tune of £5,650 per child per year. As I say, that amount will total £15 million per year, paid for through cuts elsewhere. It's not fair, it's not progressive, and it's certainly not left wing. You're standing up for millionaires, you're not standing up for Wales.

you're not standing up for Wales. And indeed, you're standing beside the Tories in wanting the same policy. So, who stole this policy from whom? Did you steal it from the Tories, or did Kemi Badenoch steal it from yourself? And why won't you use £15 million a year instead to support those who are facing the toughest of times in the cost-of-living crisis, not the richest?

The Member knows, of course, that it's not millionaires that we're talking about here through universalism, but it's hard-working families, medium earners, middle earners who the Member says should be excluded from childcare. I just don't believe that. I believe in the principle of universalism that Labour used to believe in. What has Labour become if Labour now are genuinely asking us to engage in a fundamental debate on the question of universalism? We could allow, could we not, millionaires to buy their own health services, and we don't mind, right? Let's have just a health service for those who can't afford it. I don't believe that is the best way forward. I don't believe in having a two-tier health service. I believe in the principles laid down by Aneurin Bevan I think that are as relevant today as they were when he established the NHS. So, whether it's on free school meals, or on free prescriptions, or on bus passes, or on the NHS itself, universalism is a principle that brings us together as a community, as society, and we will pursue this in the interest of the people of Wales.
Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig—Darren Millar.

Can I put on record that the thoughts of my party are with the Jewish community in Wales and around the world as we mark the anniversary of the 7 October attacks this week?

First Minister, Wales is in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. At a time when households are struggling with prices, last week the cost of alcohol in Wales went up, with a massive increase of 30 per cent in minimum alcohol pricing. And that doesn't affect just people who have alcohol problems. It affects everyone, including those people who are responsible drinkers, hitting them in their pockets too. What consideration has the Welsh Government given to the economic impact of the change in minimum alcohol pricing, especially on retailers close to the Welsh border, who are now seeing their customers nipping across into England in order to do their shopping to avoid these extra costs?

I was part of the committee in the Senedd before last that assessed the pros and cons of introducing minimum alcohol pricing. There were others here who were on that committee with me. And what we concluded was that, just as with cigarettes, the impact of pricing can have a positive impact on the choices that people make in relation to their use of alcohol. It's not a ban of alcohol; it's a trigger to make people think. That is the principle that led to the increase now— exactly these arguments that if it's about making sure that alcohol is as cheap as it possibly can be, that is not in the interest of the health of the people of Wales. It really isn't. And I think there has been a greater understanding in recent years, as happened with smoking decades ago, that we can no longer ignore the detrimental impacts of alcohol on health. And this measure is one step where we can try to redress the balance there.

Look, we all know that left-wing Governments make choices which drive people to drink. [Laughter.] But then, pushing the price of booze up isn't, I think, the right thing to do, particularly during a cost-of-living crisis. We've seen fuel prices go up, energy prices have just gone up, and now the cost of booze in Wales is up. Now, people who enjoy a responsible tipple across Wales are absolutely furious by this decision. The evidence from the Welsh Government's own evaluation undertaken in January 2025 shows that, actually, this policy isn't working. Those people who are already alcohol-dependent and problem drinkers are still alcohol-dependent, still have problems with booze, and actually they're now even worse off because they're giving up food, they're not putting the heating on, in order to pay for more expensive alcohol.

So, can I ask you, can I urge you, to look at that evidence? Instead of pushing up shopping bills, instead of punishing responsible drinkers, instead of retailers losing out because of this policy, why don't you scrap this policy altogether and get on instead in investing in support for problem drinkers, including better access to alcohol rehabilitation services in Wales?
The truth of the matter

The truth of the matter is that when we discussed this at source back then in committee, it was about doing both. There was a recognition that this wasn't a measure that would stop alcoholics from obtaining alcohol because they are addicted to alcohol. That is not what this is about. I agree that we need to be strengthening support for people who have alcohol abuse problems.

For the Member, though, to point to this decision being about the impact of the cost of living, I would ask him to reflect on the actions of successive Conservative Governments on a UK level, which decided to go down the route of austerity, hitting ordinary people in their pockets every single day in all aspects of their lives, rather than punishing the bankers who had put us in that position at that time. There are many decisions that Governments can take where we consider the impact on the pockets of the people that we represent. Minimum alcohol pricing is about health.
Y Cynnig Gofal Plant
3. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i sicrhau bod ei chynnig gofal plant yn hyblyg ac yn diwallu anghenion rhieni? OQ64647
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 3. What is the Welsh Government doing to ensure that its childcare offer is flexible and meets the needs of parents? OQ64647

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Funded childcare must be flexible for families and deliverable for providers. We're working with local authorities and registered providers to expand provision sustainably and move to a simpler system that is easier for parents to navigate. As we introduce our universal childcare offer, we will ensure that it will enable longer and more flexible sessions.

Diolch, Brif Weinidog. I'd like to give an example of how the current system isn't flexible for parents. One nursery I know of in Cardiff can only provide Flying Start provision for two and a half hours a day for the children who are eligible, but, meanwhile, the same nursery group in Newport can provide Flying Start in blocks so that parents can return to work part-time and use their Flying Start hours all in a couple of days. Parents in Cardiff aren't offered the same opportunities. Currently, funded childcare provision is too fragmented. It's a postcode lottery between local authorities and even different sides of the street. Too many who need it cannot access it.

Labour are complaining about a universal childcare offer. We've heard it again today: Labour complaining about universal childcare. The party of Aneurin Bevan and universal healthcare is complaining about universalism. They've lost touch with their roots. Meanwhile, Reform in England are closing publicly funded nurseries. So, does the First Minister agree with me that the universality of this childcare offer is key so that parents can get back to work and not a single child slips through that gap in provision?

That universality is very, very important and, as we've touched on already today, it is a broader principle that we should value.

On flexibility, as we introduce a radical and ambitious new national childcare offer, we're working to create a simpler, more streamlined system that gives parents more flexibility and easier access to funded childcare across Wales. Universal provision, of course, supports every child to get the best start in life, and thousands of low-earning families who have previously been locked out of any childcare or early-year support will benefit as a result of our policy. Current guidance allows childcare sessions to be combined. We know this flexibility is interpreted and applied differently, and we are working to, as we roll out the childcare offer, partner with local authorities and others to make sure that that consistency does become the norm across the board.

Brif Weinidog, last week your Deputy First Minister told me that childcare must be flexible for families and deliverable for providers. Yet, when I asked what this expanded offer will actually cost, she told me that the figures will only become clear in the forthcoming draft budget. But flexibility has a price tag. Longer hours, greater capacity, rural provision and the workforce to deliver it cannot be paid for with aspiration. So, how can your Government promise parents a flexible childcare offer when it still cannot tell them or this Senedd what the fully modelled policy will cost? Surely you cost the flexibility before you promise it, rather than promise it first and work out the bill afterwards. Because however flexible the promise, First Minister, the budget remains stubbornly inflexible. Eventually the numbers will have to add up. So, please reassure us that Welsh parents will not be left quite as baffled by your childcare maths as your Deputy First Minister apparently was by mine.

Well, I fundamentally disagree with that take from the Member. We've made it clear. In fact, we have put the money in for the first phase, which is the rolling out of the 12.5 hours in every part of Wales within this first financial year. It's £55 million, and that is—well, that's happening. The money has gone. It's £55 million. Working towards the end of roll-out in a Government term, you're talking about a significant sum, £300 million to £400 million, depending on uptake and so on. There are lots of different factors. But this was

But this was meant to be, and is being, done in a phased way, which is the only way that it can be done. It's not just because of the money; one of the big challenges that we are facing, and dealing with, is the workforce. We visited a nursery in Rhyl last week, and there's real excitement about how to bring more young people into the profession, which we will need to do in significant numbers to roll out this childcare offer, which will transform lives.

First Minister, we've heard from Kiera Marshall very clearly that access to childcare is heavily dependent on where you live; Flying Start is a great example. So, you are declaring—your Government says that its new offer will be flexible and responsive to parents' needs, which is great, but is that really going to take effect? We talked about rural-proofing earlier. Will rural-proofing enable this to happen in our rural communities? Can we truly see a levelling-up and a universality, as you said, of childcare in those most hard-to-reach areas like I represent?

—[Inaudible.]—rural-proofing and Flying Start, I'll maybe bring those two together. Flying Start has done a great job in helping families who are struggling to make ends meet in some parts of Wales. I know of parts in my own constituency, and many others will have their own experiences, of families who are outside Flying Start areas in rural areas who are unable to get that kind of support. What we're doing in building on Flying Start, not cutting it, is making sure that we are expanding this universally to all people, universally to all areas, because we have identified this as something that could be the underpinnings of education, job opportunities and tackling poverty. We're not setting simple targets for ourselves here. We're stretching ourselves because we think it's important, and rurality is very much a part of the mix.
Economi Cymru
4. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o effaith chwaraeon proffesiynol ar economi Cymru? OQ64617
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 4. What assessment has the First Minister made of the impact of professional sport on the Welsh economy? OQ64617

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Professional sport makes a significant contribution to the Welsh economy. It brings visitors into our communities, supports local businesses, creates jobs and showcases Wales to a global audience, at home and abroad. I'll take the opportunity to congratulate Elfyn Evans again on waving the flag in Sardinia on Sunday. But, from the Tour de France grand départ to Euro 2028, Wales has shown that it is able to attract world-class sporting events. What we need to do always is make sure that those events leave a lasting legacy for communities across Wales.

Thank you, First Minister. I agree with you: sport can have a huge impact on the economy, as we've seen in places like Swansea when they made the Premier League, with tens of millions of pounds put into the economy there; and here in Cardiff, when they were a part of the Premier League. We've seen success with Wrexham having an impact on their economy, in Newport and with other sports as well, like when the Ryder Cup came to Wales, and we've seen it when the wrestling was in Cardiff. But, what future plans has the Welsh Government got to encourage more of these large-scale events that can bring better, high-paying jobs during those periods and that can boost our hospitality industry, but not only to current areas that are seeing that? How about seeing whether we can attract more of these large-scale events to other parts of Wales yet to be showcased around the world?

I believe in the principle of seeing what we can do to attract events. We've got the Women's Champions League final coming to Cardiff. It's not always Government that delivers them. Government can be a facilitator and Government can be a conduit for making them happen. We want to work with others when they see opportunities to bring global sporting events to Wales. Like having overseas offices, it is all part of that work of raising Wales's profile on the world stage, and the benefits that flow from that are multiple. This soft diplomacy, plus the hard numbers of where we can attract, through sporting events, international inward investment, is something that we should embrace, all of us here, because Wales can only win from this.

Brif Weinidog, I'd like to focus on the people behind the sports. Every sporting journey is built on dedication, discipline and enormous personal sacrifice, whether or not an athlete ultimately reaches the highest level of success or even achieves financial success. Being an elite athlete is a unique way of life because, for many, their lives are structured around training, competition, travel, performance targets, coaches and team mates, often from a very young age. Education and career opportunities can be shaped around that commitment too, making the transition out of sport particularly challenging. While just a small number go on to

small number go on to gain financial security, many athletes make significant sacrifices without that sustainable living that comes afterwards. Yet, many do leave sport with valuable skills in leadership, resilience, discipline, teamwork and performing under pressure, skills that can only benefit the wider Welsh economy and inspire future generations. So, Prif Weinidog, what support is the Welsh Government providing to support athletes transitioning into sustainable careers when they leave professional sport?

Llywydd, I know the Member speaks from her own experience working in sports governance before being elected here. But I'd say that, through our investments as a Government in elite sports, we support partners, including Sport Wales and other governing bodies, to help athletes prepare for life beyond sport, through education, through training and through career development opportunities. There are so many of them—Welsh Athletics, Swim Wales, Hoci Cymru—they all support athletes to gain coaching, officiating and leadership qualifications alongside their sporting careers. Many former elite athletes go on to become coaches, performance managers, board members and ambassadors within their sports. The Football Association of Wales is particularly good at being a centre of excellence for preparing the coaches of the future, not just for Wales, but for other nations too. And developing that pipeline is key, I think, to ensuring that the skills, the experience and the inspiration gained through representing Wales or competing in elite sports continue to benefit our economy, our communities and our sporting success in future.

I'm a Swansea City AFC supporter and I remember the effect that playing in the premiership, winning the league cup and qualifying in Europe had on the image of Swansea. I drove down Mumbles Road one Saturday morning and a huge crowd of Chelsea supporters were walking towards the city centre. They had stayed in Swansea overnight, paid for accommodation, food and drink, helping our economy. The Ospreys, when they have European games against French and English opponents, also generate a substantial number of overnight supporters, with the same effect. Does the First Minister agree with me that the success of professional sport is beneficial for our economy, and that Swansea needs Swansea City back in the premiership and a successful Ospreys team? [Laughter.]

Right then, I'm going to have to be careful here. 'Yes' is the answer to the question. I have no doubt that professional sporting events, which happen week in, week out, of course, through professional sport in football and rugby, can bring huge, huge benefits, and supporting those hospitality sectors that support those coming to support their teams, that's something that we should encourage always.

Do I want to see Swansea City being promoted to the premier league? Absolutely, yes. As a Cardiff City FC fan, they can only go up if we go up as well, and let's make it Wrexham also. Because, genuinely, I think the success of Welsh football currently—. I see Jayne Bryant looking at me here—I wish Newport all the very, very best too, and all league of Wales teams [Laughter.] But no, I think the success of our football teams is something that we can all celebrate, whichever colour we individually choose to wear.

First Minister, as you said, professional sport plays an important role in supporting local economies by creating jobs and generating investment in our communities. One good example is the expansion of the Novira Cymru Premier football league to 16 teams, with new branding, improved broadcasting and a stronger media presence, which has raised the profile and visibility of the league, which is indeed very welcome.

Now, this season, Haverfordwest County AFC has adopted a hybrid model, combining full-time professional players with part-time players. The aim is to provide a pathway for local talent into senior football, while also further improving the club's competitiveness, building on its recent qualification for European competition, which has happened twice in recent years. So, in light of the economic impact that clubs can have on their communities, what further steps can the Welsh Government take to promote the Novira Cymru Premier football league and the clubs that actually compete in it, particularly in developing home-grown talent, strengthening their commercial profile and helping more Welsh clubs compete successfully on the European stage?

Llywydd, I hope you've built lots of time into this, because everybody wants to name their local football team now, I think. But I wish Haverfordwest well.

I'm quite excited about premier football in Wales. Currently, there's been a lot of investment and there seems to be a real vibrancy around football at its highest level in Wales.

around football at its highest level in Wales. I congratulate the work that the Football Association of Wales are doing. We engage with the Football Association of Wales in many different ways in supporting grass-roots sport, and we are happy to engage in any way that could see Welsh Government supporting facilitating the kind of investment that I know the FAW are determined to bring into Welsh football.

5. Pa gynnydd y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o ran gwella mynediad amserol at ofal y GIG? OQ64675
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 5. What progress has the First Minister made on improving timely access to NHS care? OQ64675

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Our programme for government commits us to cutting waiting lists and building a health and care service fit for the future. Backed by £145 million of additional investment, we're taking immediate action to reduce waits for diagnosis and treatment, while accelerating the wider transformation of services, with a stronger focus on prevention, care closer to home and the needs of individuals and communities.

First Minister, I'm sure you'll agree with me that when it comes to dentistry, it's important to drill into the data. Recent data shows that only 40 per cent of people were treated under an NHS dentist, a 40 per cent drop since 2020. It is very difficult for anybody now to access NHS dental treatment. Your own health Minister admitted in a committee recently that he faces a 60 mile round trip to see his dentist. When the flawed dental new contract came into force on 1 April, five practices in my area of Monmouthshire Torfaen stopped providing NHS care. Access to NHS dentists is absolutely vital, otherwise Wales will face more dental problems further down the road. What are you going to do about it, First Minister? Will you finally involve practising dentists to try and help to solve this problem, as the lack of accessibility for NHS dentists is now out of control?

The lack of accessibility to dentists is something that deeply worries me. I lost my NHS dentist a long, long time ago, as many of us here have done, I know. What we're in the process of doing now is reviewing the contract. We need to make sure that we have a system that works for the patient and for the dentist, who we want to work within the NHS system in Wales.

There's more beside that. We need to be making sure that we have that pipeline of dentists coming through the system, and that is why work led by the now Minister for local government, when she was in opposition, to bring a new dental school to Wales is something that is so, so key. The problems in dentistry are plain for all to see. I do believe we have a window in which we can try to act now, but be in no doubt about the scale of the challenge that we face around dentistry because of the legacy of a lack of attention to this over many, many years, I fear.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 6. What are the Welsh Government's plans for addressing poverty in this Senedd term? OQ64674

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Throughout our ambitious programme for government, we commit to take action to reduce financial pressures facing households, working to break the cycle of poverty that too many find themselves in. Our new child poverty strategy will set clear targets and milestones to drive ambitious, deliverable change. We'll also seek to introduce the Cynnal child payment pilot. This Government will help those in crisis, while taking longer term, strategic action to prevent people falling into poverty in the first place.

It's fascinating that your answer did not explicitly state whether you're talking about absolute poverty or relative poverty, and they are very different metrics. Absolute poverty focuses on the welfare of the poorest people in our society, something I want to see all Governments focus on. The other, relative poverty, is in reality a type of inequality, focused on the gap in wealth between people, and that can be a very dangerous metric. As Margaret Thatcher said, those who focus on inequality above absolute poverty would rather the poor were poorer so long as the rich were even less rich, reducing the gap. First Minister, do you accept there is an important difference in the two measures of poverty, and to avoid confusion in future, will you and your Government, when referencing poverty, state clearly whether you're talking about absolute poverty or the socialist obsession that is inequality?
